1:
**Sub-item 1 — Accesses all elements of board[targetRow] (no bounds error)**

Award the point whenever the response contains at least one actual repetition construct — an indexed `for`/`while` or an enhanced `for` — whose range covers every element of `board[targetRow]` with correct bounds, i.e., the traversal holds `targetRow` fixed as the row index and varies the column index across the full length of that row (or is an enhanced for over `board[targetRow]`). This item is effectively about the correctness of the loop range, not about what the body does: no_deduct even if the body never actually writes `board[targetRow][i]` or never dereferences the element, and no_deduct if the loop variable or the accessed element is unused. A missing dereference is penalized under sub-items 2–5, not here. Likewise, no_deduct if the traversal is a superset — nested loops over the whole board, or an enhanced for over `board` with an inner enhanced for over each row — since extra accesses to other rows are irrelevant to this criterion, so long as every element of `board[targetRow]` is covered with proper bounds. A bounds error elsewhere in the response does not cost this point: one complete, correctly bounded traversal of the target row suffices, even if a separate loop (e.g., an extra pairwise loop that over-runs, or a bad traversal of another row) is faulty.

Deduct if there is no loop at all covering the row (e.g., only a single hard-coded element access), if the only traversal of the target row has a bounds error so that it misses elements or runs past the end, or if the traversal walks a column instead of the row — for example indexing `board[i][targetRow]` or otherwise varying the row index with `targetRow` used as the column. Unlike sub-items 3–5, this criterion names `board[targetRow]` specifically and grants no leniency for confusing rows and columns, so a row/column swap means the elements of `board[targetRow]` were not accessed.
2:
Award this point whenever the response invokes `getColor` or `getPoints` at least once on an element of the 2D `board` array that is a `Space` object — i.e., the call is syntactically a method call on a `Space` retrieved from the array (e.g., `board[r][c].getColor()`). The point survives an incorrect access of the 2D array element or a bounds error on that access, so long as the call itself is made on a Space drawn from the array. Do not deduct based on what the response does with the returned value: comparing colors with `==` or `!=`, storing the result in a variable of the wrong type, or discarding the result entirely is out of scope here and is penalized, if at all, under sub-items 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Deduct only if the response never calls `getColor` or `getPoints` at all, calls it incorrectly (wrong name, wrong signature/arguments), calls it on something that is not a `Space` object (e.g., on the board itself, on a row array, or on a `String`/`int`), or never accesses the 2D array at all.
4:
**Sub-item 4 (initializes point variable and accumulates points in the context of a loop):**

Award the point whenever the response (a) initializes a points/sum variable and (b) inside an actual iterative construct — a `for`, enhanced-`for`, or `while` loop — makes a recognizable attempt to retrieve a space's point value and assign/add it into that variable. The only hard failures are failing to initialize the point variable at all and failing to call the point method at all; everything else about the arithmetic is merely "an incorrect sum" and is forgiven.

Concretely, do **not** deduct when: the retrieval call is malformed — a wrong method name (`getPointValue()`, `points()`), direct field access (`board[r][c].points`), a wrong receiver (`board.getPoints(r, c)`), or wrong/extra arguments — so long as the retrieved value is accumulated in a loop; the summand added is a count or constant rather than the returned point value, provided the point method is called on a space somewhere in the response; the loop may exit early via a `return` or `break` so that not every space in the target row is visited, provided each visited space's value is added to the initialized accumulator; the accumulation is overwrite-style assignment rather than a true running total, or the accumulator is declared inside the loop body; or the enclosing method does not compile (e.g., no return on every path) — this sub-item is judged on the presence of the init-plus-in-loop-accumulation code alone, independent of whether the surrounding method is legal Java.

**Deduct** when there is no initialized points variable, when no attempt whatsoever is made to retrieve a space's point value, or when the initialization-plus-accumulation pattern does not occur within an actual loop — e.g., a hardcoded unrolled sum such as `sum = board[r][0].getPoints() + board[r][1].getPoints() + board[r][2].getPoints();`, a stream/`reduce` one-liner, or accumulation done only through recursion — since these do not satisfy "in the context of a loop."
5:
**Sub-item 5 — "Determines whether all considered spaces are the same color (algorithm)"**

Judge only two things: (a) whether the response compares the colors of distinct Space objects inside an explicit loop written in the response, and (b) whether the aggregation logic itself keeps every considered space in play. Award the point when the response, inside an explicit `for`, enhanced-`for`, or `while` loop, compares each visited space's color against a reference color (or against its neighbor), covering the full line of spaces it sets out to consider.

Deduct only for these structural failures: there is no explicit loop in the shown code over the spaces being compared (recursion, stream/library traversals such as `Arrays.stream(...).allMatch(...)`, calls to a helper method whose body is not shown, or unrolled/hard-coded comparisons of fixed indices all fail this sub-item); an early return truncates the traversal so that not all spaces are considered; or the response counts matching pairs and then compares that count against an expected count that is inconsistent with the number of pairs the loop actually examines.

Everything else is excused here. Do not deduct because the loop walks the wrong dimension or uses transposed indices (e.g., `board[col][targetRow]` bounded by `board.length` instead of `board[targetRow][col]` bounded by `board[targetRow].length`) — as long as it iterates over a full line of distinct Space objects and compares each one's color to a reference color, the row/column mix-up is an indexing defect charged elsewhere. Do not deduct for an off-by-one or other index/bound slip that silently skips a space (e.g., `c < board[row].length - 1` while comparing each space to `board[row][0]`, or starting at index 1 and never comparing index 0), or for reaching beyond bounds; the rubric explicitly excuses bounds errors. Do not deduct for comparing colors with `==`/`!=` instead of `.equals` — that is charged under sub-item 3 only. Do not deduct for defects outside the color-comparison logic, such as resetting the point accumulator inside the loop (`sum = 0;` as the first statement of the body) or a method with a missing return on some path, provided the loop still visits every space and compares each color to the reference. Finally, do not deduct based on how the determination is ultimately recorded or used: whether the boolean flag is set in the inverted direction, gets overwritten, or feeds the wrong return value is judged under sub-item 6, not here.
6:
**Sub-item 6 grading note.** Award this point whenever the response's returned value is built by the right algorithm: it accumulates the points of the spaces it visits in the target row and returns either that sum or the doubled sum depending on some boolean about whether the spaces share a color. Two kinds of flaws are explicitly forgiven here, because they are charged elsewhere or covered by the item's own allowance.

First, do not deduct for off-by-one or other loop-bound/bounds errors in the summation loop (e.g., a loop that stops one element short or runs one past the end of the row). Such errors are penalized under the bounds/access sub-item, not here; so long as the algorithm correctly adds each *visited* space's points for the target row and returns the appropriate (possibly doubled) total, sub-item 6 is earned.

Second, do not deduct for a wrong use of the same-color result in the return. If both branches — the plain sum and the doubled sum — are present and the response returns one of them based on some boolean about color, the point stands even if the condition is inverted (it doubles when the colors differ) or the boolean itself was computed incorrectly; the allowance "incorrectly determine whether all spaces in the row are the same color" covers any flaw in deciding which branch is taken.

Deduct only when the returned value is not the correct point value of the target row for reasons outside those two allowances: the point variable is initialized incorrectly (e.g., to something other than 0), spaces other than those in the target row are summed, the sum is computed over a column instead of a row, the sum is computed incorrectly for reasons unrelated to loop bounds (e.g., adding the wrong quantity, overwriting rather than accumulating, doubling or scaling individual terms), the response fails to return the computed value or fails to return in some case, an early return makes it return an incorrect point value, only one of the two branches exists so the doubling is simply absent rather than misapplied, or the result is printed instead of or in addition to being returned.
